objectives: Reason about cost estimation + risk management.

slides.title: Project delivery + the lifecycle
slides.body:
**Construction project lifecycle**:
1. **Concept + planning**: needs, feasibility, environmental, permits.
2. **Design**: schematic → design development → construction documents.
3. **Bidding/procurement**: tender, evaluate bids, contract.
4. **Construction**: build.
5. **Commissioning + close-out**: handover.
6. **Operations + maintenance**: long-term.
7. **End of life / decommissioning**.

**Delivery methods**:
- **Design-Bid-Build (DBB)**: traditional. Owner contracts designer, then separately contracts builder via competitive bid. Sequential. Most public projects.
- **Design-Build (DB)**: owner contracts one team for both design + construction. Faster; single point of responsibility. Growing share.
- **Construction Manager at Risk (CM at Risk, CMAR, GMP)**: CM joins design team early; commits to GMP (Guaranteed Maximum Price). Hybrid.
- **Integrated Project Delivery (IPD)**: owner, designer, builder share risk + reward. Multi-party contract. Emerging.
- **Public-Private Partnerships (P3, PPP)**: private sector finances, designs, builds, operates infrastructure for long-term contract. Highways, hospitals, airports.

**Parties + roles**:
- **Owner**: who pays. Public agency, private developer, corporation.
- **Designer (architect + engineers)**: prepares drawings + specifications.
- **Contractor (general or prime)**: builds. Subcontracts trades.
- **Subcontractors**: specialty (electrical, mechanical, concrete, etc.).
- **Construction manager**: agent of owner, may also be at-risk.
- **Suppliers**: materials + equipment.
- **Surety**: bonds (performance, payment).
- **Inspectors + jurisdictions**: code enforcement.

**Documents**:
- **Construction drawings**: graphical.
- **Specifications**: written technical requirements. CSI MasterFormat divisions.
- **General conditions** + **supplementary conditions**: legal terms.
- **Cost estimates**: preliminary → detailed.
- **Schedule**: when activities happen.
- **Submittals**: contractor proposes materials + shop drawings; designer approves.
- **RFIs (Requests for Information)**: questions during construction.
- **Change orders**: modifications to scope/cost/schedule.

**Modern**:
- **BIM (Building Information Modeling)**: 3D models with all data. Revit, ArchiCAD, Tekla. Used for design, fabrication, construction, FM (facilities management).
- **4D BIM**: model + schedule.
- **5D BIM**: + cost.
- **6D**: + sustainability.
- **7D**: + facilities management.
- **Digital twins**: live model of operating asset.
- **Drones, lidar, photogrammetry**: as-built monitoring.
- **AR/VR**: design review + training.
- **Modular + prefab**: factory-built modules; site assembly.
- **3D-printed concrete**: emerging; full houses printed in 24 hours.

slides.title: CPM scheduling + earned value
slides.body:
**Critical Path Method (CPM)**: standard schedule planning.

Project = network of ACTIVITIES with DURATION + DEPENDENCIES.

Dependencies:
- **Finish-to-Start (FS)**: A finishes before B starts. Default.
- **Start-to-Start (SS)**: B can start when A starts.
- **Finish-to-Finish (FF)**: A + B must finish together.
- **Start-to-Finish (SF)**: rare.

**Forward + backward pass** through the network:
- **Early Start (ES) + Early Finish (EF)**: forward pass; earliest possible.
- **Late Start (LS) + Late Finish (LF)**: backward pass; latest without delaying project.
- **Total Float (TF) = LS - ES = LF - EF**: how much slack.
- **Free Float**: how much without delaying immediate successor.

**Critical path**: sequence with zero total float. Any delay here delays project. Manage tightly.

**Non-critical activities**: have float. Can shift within float window.

**Software**: Microsoft Project, Primavera P6 (oracle, standard for large projects), Asta Powerproject, ProjectLibre, etc.

**Schedule compression**:
- **Fast-track**: overlap design + construction phases. Or overlap activities normally sequential.
- **Crashing**: add resources to critical activities. Trade money for time.
- **Resource leveling**: smooth resource demand. May extend schedule.

**Risks to schedule**:
- Weather (especially earthwork, exterior).
- Long-lead items (specialty equipment).
- Permits + approvals delays.
- Labor availability.
- Material price + availability.
- Site conditions (differing geo, contamination).
- Owner changes.

**Earned Value Management (EVM)**: combine cost + schedule.
- **Planned Value (PV / BCWS)**: budget for work scheduled.
- **Earned Value (EV / BCWP)**: budget for work PERFORMED.
- **Actual Cost (AC / ACWP)**: actual cost incurred.
- **Schedule Variance (SV) = EV - PV**: positive = ahead.
- **Cost Variance (CV) = EV - AC**: positive = under budget.
- **CPI = EV/AC**: cost performance index. Above 1 = good.
- **SPI = EV/PV**: schedule performance index. Above 1 = good.
- **Estimate at Completion (EAC) = BAC / CPI**: forecast final cost.

Federal projects + many large projects require EVM reporting (DCMA, EIA-748).

slides.title: Cost estimation + risk + the future
slides.body:
**Cost estimation accuracy by phase**:
- **Order-of-magnitude (OOM)** at concept: ±50%.
- **Conceptual** at schematic design: ±30%.
- **Budget** at design development: ±15%.
- **Definitive** at construction documents: ±10%.
- **Detailed** by trade: ±5%.

**Estimating methods**:
- **Square-foot / unit cost**: \$/SF or \$/unit. Early phases.
- **Parametric**: cost = f(parameters). E.g., bridge cost as function of length + span.
- **Assembly / system**: breakdown by building system (foundation, framing, MEP).
- **Detailed quantity takeoff (QTO)**: every material + labor item.
- **Subcontractor pricing**: bid out trades.

**Resources**:
- **RSMeans**: standard cost data.
- **State DOT bid data**: historical.
- **Subcontractor relationships**: most-accurate for specific local markets.
- **AI + ML estimating**: emerging; pattern-match from historical projects.

**Bidding**:
- **Competitive (low bid)**: cheapest qualified wins. Public projects.
- **Best value**: combine cost + quality + experience.
- **Negotiated**: with selected contractor.
- **Reverse auction**: live bidding event.

**Risk management**:
- **Identify**: brainstorm + checklists.
- **Assess**: probability × impact.
- **Plan**: avoid, mitigate, transfer (insurance, contract), accept.
- **Monitor**: throughout project.

**Common risks**:
- Cost overruns (almost universal at some level).
- Schedule delays.
- Quality defects → rework.
- Safety incidents.
- Disputes + claims.
- Force majeure (COVID).
- Material price volatility.

**Disputes + claims**:
- Causes: changes, delays, differing site conditions, defective design, contract ambiguities.
- Resolution: negotiation → mediation → arbitration → litigation.
- Notice provisions in contracts critical.

**Safety**:
- USA construction: ~1000 deaths/year (industry leader in fatalities). 'Fatal four': falls, struck-by, electrocution, caught-in-between.
- OSHA regulations.
- Toolbox talks, PPE, training, fall protection.
- Modern: drone inspection (no workers at heights), exoskeletons, sensors.

**Sustainability**:
- **LEED, BREEAM, Living Building Challenge**: certifications.
- **Embodied carbon**: emissions from materials production. Increasingly tracked.
- **Carbon-neutral / Net-Zero**: targets for new buildings.
- **Adaptive reuse**: renovate existing > new construction.
- **Material passport**: track materials for future reuse.

**Modern construction**:
- **Prefab + modular**: factory production, site assembly. Marriott opening new hotels in months not years.
- **3D printing**: walls, full small buildings.
- **Robotics**: bricklayer robots, drone-based survey, autonomous earth moving (Built Robotics).
- **AI**: design generation, cost prediction, schedule optimization, safety monitoring.
- **Decarbonization**: green steel + cement, electric equipment, on-site renewables.

**Productivity**: construction productivity has stagnated for decades while other industries (manufacturing, agriculture) grew. McKinsey + others identify large opportunity for digitization + modernization. Industry slowly transforming.

question.question: Apply CPM to a small project
question.goal: 5 activities: A (3 days), B (5), C (4), D (2), E (3). Dependencies: A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→E. Find critical path + duration.

steps.prompt: A is the first task. After A, both B + C can start in parallel. Then D needs both. Then E. Compute durations through each path: A-B-D-E vs A-C-D-E.

options: A-B-D-E: 3+5+2+3 = 13 days. A-C-D-E: 3+4+2+3 = 12 days. Critical: A-B-D-E (longest).

steps.reveal: A, B, D, E. Float = 0. Delays here delay project.
1 day. C can slip up to 1 day without delaying project.

steps.prompt: If you can compress only ONE activity by 1 day, which has biggest project-finish impact?

options: Any critical activity (A, B, D, or E). Compressing C doesn't help — it has float. Compress critical path activities for shortest project.

steps.reveal: Compress critical path activities to shorten project. Compressing non-critical does NOTHING for total duration (just increases float). Standard fast-track + crashing focus on critical path.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Critical path = longest path = project duration; only compressing critical path helps}}$$ CPM is the foundation of construction scheduling. Real projects have thousands of activities + complex networks; software (P6) computes critical path + tracks progress + variance. Modern: 4D BIM links schedule to model; visualizes sequence. Linear scheduling for repetitive work (highways, tunnels). Lean construction principles minimize waste + variability.

question.question: Why do mega-projects (Boston Big Dig, California HSR, Berlin BER) routinely overrun budgets + schedules?
options: Multiple causes: optimistic initial estimates (often political, to get approval), scope creep, unforeseen conditions (geological, environmental, archaeological), changes in requirements, design errors, contract disputes, supply-chain issues, political delays. Bent Flyvbjerg's research: 'megaprojects pathology' — strategic misrepresentation, optimism bias, planning fallacy. Documented across hundreds of projects globally.
question.explanation:
Flyvbjerg (Oxford prof, megaproject expert) documents systemic megaproject failure across all sectors + countries. Average overrun: 28% cost, 70% schedule. Big Dig (Boston): 3× original budget. California HSR: years late, costs ballooning. Berlin BER airport: 9 years late, 3× budget. Causes: (1) Strategic misrepresentation (low-ball estimates to win approval). (2) Optimism bias. (3) Planning fallacy. (4) Genuine unknowns (geological, market, technology). (5) Decision-maker turnover. (6) Inadequate front-end planning.

Successful mega-projects (some Australian highway P3s, some Norwegian fjord tunnels, Hong Kong airport): better planning, qualified contractors, risk sharing, governance. Reference-class forecasting (compare to similar past projects) reduces bias. Industry slowly maturing on lessons.

slides.workedSolution: Strategic misrepresentation + optimism bias + planning fallacy + genuine unknowns. Documented systematically (Flyvbjerg). Improvements: reference-class forecasting (similar past projects), risk-sharing contracts, qualified P3 partners, governance, front-end planning. Slowly improving but pervasive. Modern AI may help estimating + risk analysis.

question.question: Design-Build vs Design-Bid-Build
question.prompt: A municipality considers Design-Build for a new fire station to accelerate schedule. Walk through trade-offs.
Explain in two or three sentences why construction management is increasingly important as projects grow in scale + complexity.
question.rubric: Mentions that megaprojects (\$1B+) involve thousands of stakeholders + activities + risks; without rigorous management (CPM, EVM, BIM, risk register, change control), they spiral out of control; modern tools (digital twins, AI-augmented planning, BIM coordination) are reshaping the discipline. Industry productivity has lagged manufacturing for decades; modernization is the focus.
